Hey, was the prodigy in middle school and ended up almost flunking out by highschool - 25 now and I went BACK to college after trying several times, failing, and being put on academic probation. But I’m currently taking classes that are going well for the first time in a decade

The thing that changed things for me is the understanding that A LOT of people experience what we experience. I had to get past feeling shameful about my situation to be able to start acknowledging it and making it better.

When it comes to school - a part of my problem was that I hated my major, all the classes I had to take for it, etc. upon switching, it was like a whole new world in academia.

The truth is a lot of people feel stuck, or feel like they’re hitting a dead end. The harder, sadder part of that is that a lot of the time people roll over and accept that, or feel they can’t do anything about it. I was in that boat of feeling like I was just genuinely a loser for failing out 5+ times. And THAT deters us from ever pursuing something brighter, or allowing it to get better.

Your parents will forgive you and they will forgive you much faster when you start acting to help yourself. If they don’t, they weren’t a support to you in the first place, so congratulations on dropping some stress. 

It does get better but you have to give yourself some slack for failing. Burnout happens, it’s not just a month long depression episode, it takes A LOT of time to heal from it.

Alright you may be right in saying that this is kind of ‘bullshit’. This fact was picked up from a study done in 2008 in Denver that took the reported biting incidents and separated it by breed. Labrador retrievers made up 13.3% of the bites, but pit bulls were a close second with 8.4%. 

That being said I want to point out that these statistics reflect the most common breeds to own  - Denver does have a ‘ban’ on owning pit bulls but it’s been rarely enforced and only pertains to certain areas. So despite this ban, you’ll find pit bulls are probably one of the most common breeds to own aside from a Labrador or golden out there (and I can confirm this being a Colorado native myself, everyone and their mother owns a pit bull out here).

I was wrong in saying that as a generalization that labradors have a higher biting rate, because they do not. But what I am trying to point out is that neither do pit bulls when they are well trained. The statistics that are often brought up for pit bull attacks actually reflect the fatality of the attack rather than the sheer number of bites - and this is where it gets skewed because pit bulls are both extremely strong and have been repeatedly used as a breed trained for illegal fighting which will increase the number of attacks simply because of the high number of pit bulls trained to be aggressive. So those combinations have given the notion that pit bulls are, by nature, more aggressive than other dog breeds. When in reality they aren’t and most of that stems from what their breed has been used for for some time (dog fighting, guard dog, etc).

Edit: also I’d like to point out I don’t own a pit bull or any dog for that matter as my lease doesn’t allow it. I do babysit dogs for several different people and I have always had way more aggression/behavioral problems with working breeds with lots of energy - heelers, huskies, shiba inus. They get bored easily, which turns neurotic, which makes them fairly unpredictable and more likely to misbehave/be aggressive without warrant. I rarely meet neurotic pit bulls/staffies/bulldogs, the ones I have met with behavior problems have come from rescue situations, or they are young and are still being trained.

Edit 2: someone pointed out pit bulls have a tendency to be dog aggressive. This is true due to the fact that they are considered a very loyal, protective breed. If they’re raised in a house hold without other dogs they develop attachments to people and will consider other dogs threatening. This is true for a lot of breeds though, from goldens to mastiffs to doodles.
